title: How do you read XML files in Spark (`spark.read.format("com.databricks.spark.xml").option("rootTag","...").option("rowTag","...").load(...)`) and what other special formats does Spark support (JDBC, Avro, Delta, Iceberg, HBase connectors)?
shortTitle: Reading XML and other special formats in Spark

s1_definition.profdef: Spark reads XML through a data-source connector (the spark-xml package, now built into Spark 4 and available as `com.databricks.spark.xml` or format `xml` earlier) by specifying `rowTag`, the repeating element that becomes one row, and optionally `rootTag`, the wrapping element. Beyond the built-in formats (CSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC, text), Spark reads many special formats through connectors: JDBC for relational databases, Avro, Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and HBase, among others. Each is selected with `spark.read.format(...)` plus connector-specific options.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank receives data in many shapes — a messaging partner sends XML, the core banking system lives in an Oracle database, the lake stores Parquet and Delta, and a NoSQL store holds HBase rows. Spark is like a universal reader with interchangeable lenses: snap on the XML lens and tell it which tag is one record, snap on the JDBC lens and give it a connection string, snap on the Delta lens for the lake. The reading syntax is always the same shape, only the format and options change.
s1_definition.oneliner: Spark reads XML by naming the rowTag, and reads JDBC, Avro, Delta, Iceberg, and HBase through pluggable connectors, all via spark.read.format with format-specific options.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Spark reads XML through a data-source connector (the spark-xml package, now built into Spark 4 and available as `com.databricks.spark.xml` or format `xml` earlier) by specifying `rowTag`, the repeating element that becomes one row, and optionally `rootTag`, the wrapping element. Beyond the built-in formats (CSV, JSON, Parquet, ORC, text), Spark reads many special formats through connectors: JDBC for relational databases, Avro, Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, and HBase, among others. Each is selected with `spark.read.format(...)` plus connector-specific options.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank receives data in many shapes — a messaging partner sends XML, the core banking system lives in an Oracle database, the lake stores Parquet and Delta, and a NoSQL store holds HBase rows. Spark is like a universal reader with interchangeable lenses: snap on the XML lens and tell it which tag is one record, snap on the JDBC lens and give it a connection string, snap on the Delta lens for the lake. The reading syntax is always the same shape, only the format and options change.

**One line to remember:** Spark reads XML by naming the rowTag, and reads JDBC, Avro, Delta, Iceberg, and HBase through pluggable connectors, all via spark.read.format with format-specific options.

sections.s2_technical:
For XML you use the spark-xml data source. The key option is `rowTag`, the repeating element Spark turns into one row; `rootTag` names the document wrapper. For example `spark.read.format("xml").option("rowTag", "transaction").load("txns.xml")` makes each `<transaction>` element a row, mapping nested elements into struct columns and repeated elements into arrays. Other options include `attributePrefix` for XML attributes and `valueTag` for element text alongside attributes. In older Spark you reference `com.databricks.spark.xml` and add the `spark-xml` package; Spark 4 includes it natively as format `xml`.

The reader pattern generalizes. `spark.read.format("jdbc")` reads from a relational database using options `url`, `dbtable` or `query`, `user`, `password`, and a `driver`; you parallelize large reads with `partitionColumn`, `lowerBound`, `upperBound`, and `numPartitions`. `spark.read.format("avro")` reads Avro files, often paired with a schema registry in streaming. `spark.read.format("delta")` reads Delta Lake tables with time travel options. `spark.read.format("iceberg")` reads Apache Iceberg tables through its catalog. HBase is read through connectors such as the Spark-HBase connector, mapping column families to DataFrame columns.

The unifying idea is Spark's DataSource API: a format name plus options produces a DataFrame, and once loaded all data looks the same regardless of source, so the rest of your pipeline is format-agnostic. Writing mirrors reading with `df.write.format(...).save(...)` or `.jdbc(...)`.

A senior nuance: connectors are added as packages with `--packages` and must match Spark and Scala versions; for JDBC you always parallelize large pulls to avoid a single-partition bottleneck and push filters down with a `query` option; and for XML, deeply nested or irregular documents may need explicit schema to avoid inference surprises.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank receives a daily XML feed of interbank transfers from a partner, where each `<transfer>` element is one transaction. Parsing this by hand is fragile. This is exactly what spark-xml with rowTag solves.

Problem 2 — Reference account data lives in an Oracle database that must be joined to the transfers. This is exactly the JDBC reader.

Problem 3 — The output must land in the Delta lake for downstream consumers. This is exactly the Delta writer.

What the code will do: a PySpark demo (`MultiFormatDemo`) that reads an XML transfers feed with rowTag, reads accounts via JDBC, joins them for Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001), and writes the enriched result to Delta.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
multiformat-banking/
├── requirements.txt
├── data/transfers.xml
├── src/
│   ├── multiformat_demo.py      (runnable demo)
│   └── readers/
│       ├── __init__.py
│       └── source_readers.py    (xml / jdbc / delta readers)
```

##### 4b. SQL / Source Script

```sql
-- Oracle reference table read via JDBC
-- SELECT account_id, holder_name FROM core.accounts;
```

Sample `data/transfers.xml`:

```xml
<transfers>
  <transfer><txn_id>TXN-1</txn_id><account_id>SAV2001</account_id><amount>50000.00</amount></transfer>
  <transfer><txn_id>TXN-2</txn_id><account_id>CUR3001</account_id><amount>25000.00</amount></transfer>
</transfers>
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```text
# spark-defaults.conf
spark.jars.packages com.databricks:spark-xml_2.12:0.18.0,io.delta:delta-spark_2.12:3.1.0
```
sections.s4d_java:
```python
# File: src/multiformat_demo.py
# Reads XML + JDBC, joins, writes Delta for the National Bank of India.
import logging
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from readers.source_readers import read_xml_transfers, read_jdbc_accounts, write_delta

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)s %(message)s")
log = logging.getLogger("MultiFormatDemo")

def spark_session() -> SparkSession:
    return (SparkSession.builder.appName("MultiFormatDemo")
            .config("spark.sql.extensions", "io.delta.sql.DeltaSparkSessionExtension")
            .config("spark.sql.catalog.spark_catalog",
                    "org.apache.spark.sql.delta.catalog.DeltaCatalog")
            .getOrCreate())

def main() -> None:
    spark = spark_session()

    transfers = read_xml_transfers(spark, "data/transfers.xml")  # XML reader
    log.info("Transfers read from XML:")
    transfers.show()

    accounts = read_jdbc_accounts(spark)                          # JDBC reader
    log.info("Accounts read from JDBC (Oracle):")
    accounts.show()

    enriched = transfers.join(accounts, "account_id", "left")
    log.info("Enriched transfers (XML joined to JDBC accounts):")
    enriched.show()

    write_delta(enriched, "/data/warehouse/enriched_transfers")   # Delta writer
    log.info("Enriched result written to Delta lake")
    spark.stop()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
# File: src/readers/source_readers.py
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, DataFrame

def read_xml_transfers(spark: SparkSession, path: str) -> DataFrame:
    # rowTag = the repeating element that becomes one row
    return (spark.read.format("xml")
            .option("rowTag", "transfer")
            .option("rootTag", "transfers")
            .load(path))

def read_jdbc_accounts(spark: SparkSession) -> DataFrame:
    # JDBC reader with a pushdown query; parallelize large reads in production
    return (spark.read.format("jdbc")
            .option("url", "jdbc:oracle:thin:@//db-host:1521/COREDB")
            .option("query", "SELECT account_id, holder_name FROM core.accounts")
            .option("user", "analytics")
            .option("password", "${DB_PASSWORD}")
            .option("driver", "oracle.jdbc.OracleDriver")
            .load())

def write_delta(df: DataFrame, path: str) -> None:
    df.write.format("delta").mode("overwrite").save(path)
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an XML file with two `<transfer>` elements and an Oracle `accounts` table.

Step 1: `read_xml_transfers` loads the XML with `rowTag="transfer"`, so each transfer element becomes a row with columns `txn_id`, `account_id`, and `amount`. The `rootTag` wrapper is ignored for row shaping.

Step 2: `read_jdbc_accounts` opens a JDBC connection to Oracle and runs the pushdown query, returning `account_id` and `holder_name` for the accounts.

Step 3: The two DataFrames join on `account_id` with a left join, so every transfer keeps its row and gains the holder name. SAV2001 gains Rajesh Kumar, CUR3001 gains Priya Sharma.

Step 4: `write_delta` writes the enriched result to the Delta lake in overwrite mode, where downstream consumers read it with the Delta format.

Step 5: Throughout, once each source was loaded into a DataFrame, the join and write code did not care that one source was XML and another was a database — the DataSource API made them uniform.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Spark reads XML through a data-source connector, historically the spark-xml package referenced as com dot databricks dot spark dot xml and available as format xml, and now built into Spark 4. The key option is rowTag, which names the repeating element that becomes one row, and rootTag names the document wrapper. So reading a transfers file is spark dot read dot format xml, option rowTag transfer, load the path, and each transfer element becomes a row with nested elements mapped to struct columns and repeated elements to arrays. There are extra options like attributePrefix and valueTag for handling XML attributes and element text.

The important thing is that this reader pattern generalizes across many special formats through Spark's DataSource API: a format name plus options always produces a DataFrame. JDBC reads relational databases with url, dbtable or query, user, password, and driver, and I parallelize large pulls with partitionColumn and bounds. Avro reads Avro files, often with a schema registry. Delta reads Delta Lake tables with time travel. Iceberg reads Apache Iceberg through its catalog. And HBase is read through a dedicated connector that maps column families to columns. Once any of these is loaded, every source looks identical, so the rest of the pipeline is format-agnostic.

At the National Bank of India I used exactly this to combine sources. A partner sent a daily XML feed of interbank transfers, which I read with rowTag set to transfer; the reference accounts lived in Oracle, which I read with the JDBC connector and a pushdown query; I joined them to enrich each transfer with the holder name; and I wrote the result to the Delta lake for downstream teams. The practical advice I give is to add connectors with the packages flag and match them to the Spark and Scala versions, to always parallelize large JDBC reads so you do not bottleneck on one partition, and to supply an explicit schema for irregular XML so inference does not surprise you.

---

keyPoints: Parquet: columnar, compressed, schema — best for analytics
Avro: row-based, schema evolution, compact — best for Kafka
ORC: columnar, optimized for Hive — similar to Parquet
Choose: Parquet for reads (analytics), Avro for writes (streaming)
